title: Two faces of one diagonal argument
content: The module docstring states the file's thesis: Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorem and Turing's 1936 undecidability of the halting problem are the same diagonal argument seen from two angles. The parent `GodelIncompleteness` builds a self-referential sentence syntactically via the diagonal lemma; this file instead derives incompleteness as a *corollary* of undecidability — the recursion-theoretic route. The headline payoff is that no Gödel sentence need be constructed by hand: diagonalizing against the theory's own provability decider hands you an explicit independent sentence for free.
mathContext: The bridge: a complete, sound, effectively axiomatized theory would yield a decision procedure for the (undecidable) diagonal predicate $D$, so no such theory can be complete. Symbolically, $\text{undecidable}(D) \Rightarrow \neg\,\text{Complete}(T)$ for every sound effective $T$ representing $D$.
prerequisites: the notion of a formal theory

title: The diagonal predicate D
content: `D n := (run n n = false)` says 'procedure n rejects its own code'. This is the abstract halting-style predicate at the heart of both Turing undecidability and Gödel incompleteness. Modelling `run` as a total `ℕ → ℕ → Bool` is harmless: the diagonal obstruction holds for every `run`, which is exactly why the same argument powers both theorems. The self-application `run n n` (a procedure fed its own index) is the diagonal of Cantor's table.
mathContext: $D(n) \equiv [\,\mathrm{run}(n,n) = \mathsf{false}\,]$. Compare the halting predicate $H(n) \equiv [\,\varphi_n(n)\!\downarrow\,]$: both evaluate program $n$ on its own code, the Cantor-diagonal position $(n,n)$.

title: Decidability within the family
content: `DecidedBy P e := ∀ n, (run e n = true ↔ P n)` is the abstract notion 'P is computable by code e' — `run e` is the characteristic function of `P`. A theory is 'effectively axiomatized' precisely when its provability predicate is `DecidedBy` some code. Quantifying over codes *inside* the same family `run` is what lets the diagonal close: the decider is itself an object the diagonal can be evaluated at.
mathContext: $\mathrm{DecidedBy}(P, e) \equiv \forall n.\,[\mathrm{run}(e,n) = \mathsf{true} \iff P(n)]$, i.e. $\mathrm{run}(e,\cdot)$ is the indicator $\chi_P$. Effective axiomatization $=$ $\exists e.\,\mathrm{DecidedBy}(\mathrm{Provable}, e)$.

title: Turing's diagonal: D is undecidable
content: `D_undecidable` proves no code decides `D`. If `run e` were the characteristic function of `D`, instantiating `DecidedBy` at `n = e` gives `run e e = true ↔ run e e = false` — a Boolean equivalent to its own negation, impossible by `cases` on the two values. The argument is uniform over every `run`, the purest form of the halting-problem diagonal. The only foundational dependency is `propext` (which does not count as an assumption under the axiom-integrity policy), so the result remains 0-axiom / verified.
mathContext: Assume $\mathrm{run}(e,\cdot) = \chi_D$. Then $\mathrm{run}(e,e) = \mathsf{true} \iff D(e) \iff \mathrm{run}(e,e) = \mathsf{false}$ — no Boolean fixed point exists. This is Cantor's $\neg$ on the diagonal: no row equals the flipped diagonal.

title: Sound, effectively axiomatized theory
content: `SoundEffectiveTheory` bundles `Provable`, `Refutable`, two soundness fields (`sound_pos`: proving `D n` makes it true; `sound_neg`: refuting `D n` makes it false), and `decidable_provable` (provability decided by some code). It is the recursion-theoretic stand-in for 'a sound theory whose theorems are recursively enumerable'. Note these structure fields are *hypotheses*, not free axioms: the theorems are quantified over all `T : SoundEffectiveTheory`, so the conclusion is conditional on a theory satisfying them — consistent with the axiom-integrity policy (the file's headline results carry their assumptions in the theory hypothesis, not as global `axiom`s).
mathContext: A structure with $\mathrm{Provable}, \mathrm{Refutable} : \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Prop}$; soundness $\mathrm{Provable}(n)\Rightarrow D(n)$ and $\mathrm{Refutable}(n)\Rightarrow \neg D(n)$; effectiveness $\exists e.\,\mathrm{DecidedBy}(\mathrm{Provable}, e)$. This abstracts away the arithmetization of the parent's fixed encoding.

title: Soundness implies consistency
content: `sound_imp_consistent` shows that no sentence is both provable and refutable: if `Provable n` and `Refutable n` held, `sound_pos` would make `D n` true while `sound_neg` makes it false — contradiction. So the effectiveness hypothesis is not even needed for consistency; soundness alone gives it for free. This separates the cheap consequence (consistency) from the substantive one (incompleteness, which needs the diagonal).
mathContext: $\mathrm{Provable}(n) \wedge \mathrm{Refutable}(n) \Rightarrow D(n) \wedge \neg D(n) \Rightarrow \bot$. Hence a sound theory is automatically consistent: $\neg\exists n.\,(\mathrm{Provable}(n) \wedge \mathrm{Refutable}(n))$.

title: Gödel's First Incompleteness via Turing
content: `godel_via_turing` proves every sound, effectively axiomatized theory of the `D`-sentences has an EXPLICIT independent sentence. The witness is `e`, the code of the theory's own provability decider. (1) If `D e` were provable, `sound_pos` forces `run e e = false` while the decider gives `run e e = true` — contradiction. (2) If `D e` were refutable, `sound_neg` gives `¬ D e` i.e. `run e e = true`, so the decider makes `D e` provable, and `sound_pos` then makes `D e` true — contradicting `¬ D e`. No Gödel sentence is built by hand; it falls out of diagonalizing the provability predicate.
mathContext: Take $e$ with $\mathrm{DecidedBy}(\mathrm{Provable}, e)$. The sentence $D(e) = [\mathrm{run}(e,e)=\mathsf{false}]$ asserts 'the prover rejects its own code'. It is true iff unprovable, the recursion-theoretic Gödel sentence $G \leftrightarrow \neg\mathrm{Prov}(\ulcorner G\urcorner)$.

title: The explicit Gödel sentence: D e
content: `godel_sentence_independent` isolates the witness: given any code `e` that decides `Provable`, the sentence `D e` is neither provable nor refutable. This is the same argument as `godel_via_turing` but stated so the independent sentence is named explicitly — `D e` is the concrete recursion-theoretic Gödel sentence, parametrized by the decider code rather than constructed by a fixed-point lemma.
mathContext: For $e$ deciding $\mathrm{Provable}$: $\neg\mathrm{Provable}(e) \wedge \neg\mathrm{Refutable}(e)$, where $D(e)$ is the named independent sentence. It plays the role of the parent's hand-built $G$.

title: Incompleteness, stated as ¬ Complete
content: `Complete T` means every `D`-sentence is provable or refutable. `incompleteness` restates `godel_via_turing` as `¬ Complete T`: the independent sentence from the diagonal would have to be provable or refutable under completeness, contradicting both. Unlike the parent's `first_incompleteness` (one fixed encoding), this quantifies over ALL sound, effectively axiomatized theories of the `D`-sentences.
mathContext: $\mathrm{Complete}(T) \equiv \forall n.\,(\mathrm{Provable}(n) \vee \mathrm{Refutable}(n))$. The diagonal sentence violates this for every sound effective $T$, so $\neg\mathrm{Complete}(T)$ holds universally.

title: A concrete instance: the obstruction is structural
content: Part III drives home that undecidability is structural, not about the predicate being 'hard'. `no_decider_for_const_true` instantiates `D_undecidable` at the constant-`true` family, and `const_true_D_false` shows that in this family `D` is identically `False` (the empty predicate). Yet no code in the family decides the empty predicate, because every code answers `true` everywhere while a decider would need `run e n = true ↔ False`. The obstruction is the closure of the family under self-application, not the intrinsic difficulty of `D`.
mathContext: For $\mathrm{run} \equiv \lambda\,\_\,\_.\,\mathsf{true}$: $D \equiv \mathsf{False}$ (empty predicate), yet no $e$ satisfies $\mathrm{run}(e,n)=\mathsf{true} \iff \mathsf{False}$ since the LHS is always $\mathsf{true}$. Undecidability persists for the simplest possible predicate.
